subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of the normal at θ = π/3 to the hyperbola 3x² − 4y² = 12.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Set up the normal formula
steps.margin_note: First mark. The parametric point on a hyperbola is (a secθ, b tanθ).
steps.memory_tip: Hyperbola normal uses secθ, tanθ and a PLUS sign — not sinθ, cosθ and a minus sign, as an ellipse's normal does.
lines: Equation of the normal at the point P(θ)
= (a secθ, b tanθ) is: ax/secθ + by/tanθ
steps.why: The parametric point on a hyperbola is (a secθ, b tanθ); the normal formula at this point is a ready-made result, so the only work here is reading off a, b and substituting θ.
common_mistakes: Using the ellipse's normal formula (with sinθ, cosθ, and a minus sign) instead of the hyperbola's, which uses secθ, tanθ and a plus sign.
Forgetting to take the square root of b² = 3 to get b = √3.

steps.label: Substitute and simplify
steps.margin_note: Second mark. sec60° and tan60° are standard exact values.
steps.memory_tip: sec60° = 2, tan60° = √3 — both cancel neatly against a = 2, b = √3.
lines: θ = π/3: secθ = sec60° = 2, tanθ = tan60° = √3
steps.why: Substituting sec60°=2 and tan60°=√3 makes both denominators cancel neatly against a=2 and b=√3, leaving a simple linear equation.
common_mistakes: Using sec(π/3) and tan(π/3) as decimal approximations instead of the exact values 2 and √3.
Adding a² + b² as 4 + √3 instead of 4 + 3 = 7 — b² is 3, not √3.
